source_text: Et quamvis quae acta sunt, ad defensionem veritatis exuberent, tamen ad ea, quae inferimus, ut sit lector intentus, admoneo. Apparebit enim irrefutabiliter nihil in his locis apostolum Paulum de natura, sed de conversatione mortalium disputasse; vim nempe gratiae Christi et peccati primi e regione constituens comparansque effectus utriusque laboravit ostendere magis Christi profuisse mysterium quam primi hominis nocuisse peccatum. Id autem docuimus in sensu traducis non posse constare; ut ergo multa quae enumeravit, ita hoc peculiariter ad laudem voluit gratiae pertinere, quod ait: Iudicium ex uno in condemnationem, gratia autem ex multis delictis in iustificationem vitae [n151] . Quod hoc modo naturalis mali assertor exposuit: Ideo - inquit - " ex uno in condemnationem ", quia sufficiens est illud unum peccatum, quod originaliter trahitur, ad condemnationem ducere, sicut ducit parvulos, qui ex Adam nascuntur, si in Christo non renascantur, etiamsi alia peccata nulla sint. " Gratia autem ex multis delictis in iustificationem ", quia non solum illud dimittit, quod originaliter trahitur, sed etiam cetera, quae ab unoquoque motu propriae voluntatis adduntur [n152] . Ecce professus es, licet impietate Manichaea, esse quidem naturale peccatum, verumtamen unum, ob quod ais nascentes debere damnari.
pass_a_gloss: And although the things which have been done overflow toward the defense of truth, nevertheless I warn that the reader be intent toward those things which we infer. For it will appear irrefutably that in these places the apostle Paul disputed nothing about nature, but about the conversation of mortals; setting the force of the grace of Christ and of the first sin from the opposite region and comparing the effects of each he labored to show that the mystery of Christ helped more than the sin of the first human being harmed. But we have taught that this cannot stand in the sense of the tradux; as therefore many things which he enumerated, so this he wanted peculiarly to belong to the praise of grace, that he says: Judgment from one into condemnation, but grace from many offenses into justification of life. Which the asserter of a natural evil explained in this way: For this reason, he says, 'from one into condemnation,' because that one sin which is drawn originally is sufficient to lead to condemnation, as it leads little children who are born from Adam, if they are not born again in Christ, even if there are no other sins. 'But grace from many offenses into justification,' because it not only dismisses that which is drawn originally, but also the rest which are added by each one by a motion of proper will. Look, you have professed, although by Manichaean impiety, that there is indeed a natural sin, yet one, on account of which you say those being born ought to be damned.

lemmas.lexica: LS delictum; Blaise Rom 5 delictum vs donum
LS iustificatio; Blaise forensic making-just, not later system
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: Although what we have already accomplished more than suffices to defend the truth, I nevertheless urge the reader to attend to what we add. It will appear irrefutably that in these passages the apostle Paul discussed not human nature but human conduct. Setting the power of Christ’s grace and of the first sin opposite each other, and comparing the effects of both, he worked to show that Christ’s mystery helped more than the first man’s sin harmed. We have shown that this cannot hold under the interpretation of inherited transmission. Among the many points he listed, then, he intended this especially to praise grace: ‘The judgment was from one offense to condemnation, but grace is from many offenses to justification of life’ (Romans 5:16). The defender of natural evil explained this as follows: ‘It says “from one offense to condemnation” because that one sin inherited at birth is sufficient to lead to condemnation, as it leads infants born from Adam unless they are reborn in Christ, even if there are no other sins. “But grace is from many offenses to justification,” because it forgives not only the sin inherited at birth but also the other sins each person adds by the movement of his own will’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.46). See: you have professed, though with Manichaean impiety, that natural sin exists, but that it is one sin, on account of which you say newborn children must be condemned.

choices.why: Paul's delictum of the one man; an act, not a nature.
Paul's iustificatio vitae; keep forensic making-just, not a later systematic slogan as default.
